paper_metadata.title: Strengthening of Mg-Li alloy dominated by continuously hardened Mg phase during room temperature rolling

evidence.quote: The process of room temperature rolling is a straightforward and efﬁcient method for producing high strength Mg-Li alloys, but the underlying strengthening mechanism remains unclear.

For the Rolling-40%, the presence of precipitated α-Mg was also observed, as depicted in Fig. S1.
Speciﬁcally, a limited number of twins were observed within the microstructure of Rolling-40% due to the inﬂuence of room temperature rolling, as depicted in Fig. S2a and b.
The misorientation of paths AB and CD reveals a consistent misorientation observed in both common twins and matrix phases within magnesium alloys [ 41 , 42 ].
However, only a limited number of dynamic recrystallization grains were observed, and predominantly distributed along the twins.
Consequently, dislocations and low-angle grain boundaries are expected to be prevalent within the α-Mg.

The presence of a high density of dislocations stored in the Mg-phase emerges as the dominant factor contributing to improved strength in Mg-Li alloys.
In-situ compression testing reveals that ⟨ c + a ⟩ slip activation and twinning-induced slip serve as internal mechanisms for continuous deformation and hardening within the Mg-phase.
A signiﬁcant number of non-basal slips were found to be active, particularly pyramidal < a > and pyramidal ⟨ c + a ⟩ slips appear to be dominant in this region.
Twinning is also a signiﬁcant mechanism for plastic deformation in α-Mg, as illustrated in Fig. 8d .
This observation suggests that the formation of twins during the rolling process can facilitate dynamic recrystallization.
